lesson_title: Count the Twos: Five Exponent Laws in One Picture
hook_text: 2 cubed times 2 to the fourth. Is it 4 to the seventh? 2 to the twelfth? Count the twos and you will never guess again.
clip_script: Picture a box with three twos inside, all multiplied. That is 2 cubed. Next to it, a box with four twos: 2 to the fourth. Multiply the boxes and you have three twos then four more — seven twos. 2 to the seventh. The twos never became fours, so 4 to the seventh is nonsense. Divide instead: five threes over two threes, pair them off like socks, two pairs cancel, three left: 3 cubed. Wrap a box in a bracket and square it: two boxes of three twos is six twos — multiply the counts. Share an outside exponent with every factor in a product, number included: 3x all squared is 9x squared. And anything non-zero to the power zero? Halve 16, 8, 4, 2 once more: one.
visual_style: Cardboard boxes of glowing 2s slide together and merge into one longer box with a count ticking to 7; socks pair off and vanish for division; a bracket wraps a box and duplicates it; the halving sequence lands on 1.
pacing: Quick visual beats, one law per beat, with a pause on the 4-to-the-seventh trap.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and simplify any power expression without a formula sheet.
